claim: In the last decade well beyond half a million bacterial genomes have been sequenced worldwide, about 7% of these from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) strains.
source: In the last decade well beyond half a million bacterial genomes have been sequenced worldwide, about 7% of these from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) strains (Blackwell et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blackwell et al., 2021.

claim: Molecular epidemiology studies of MTB use microbial genome sequences sampled from different patients to investigate epidemiological dynamics such as transmission, relapses, and the acquisition and spread of antibiotic resistance.
source: Molecular epidemiology studies of MTB (and of other pathogens) use microbial genome sequences sampled from different patients to investigate epidemiological dynamics such as transmission, relapses, and the acquisition and spread of antibiotic resistance (Hatherell et al., 2016; Guthrie and Gardy, 2017; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hatherell et al., 2016; Guthrie and Gardy, 2017; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019.

claim: The identification of clustered MTB strains is commonly interpreted as evidence for recent local transmission, while patients infected with non-clustered strains (singletons) are thought to be novel introductions.
source: The identification of clustered MTB strains is commonly interpreted as evidence for recent local transmission, while patients infected with non-clustered strains (singletons) are thought to be novel introductions (i.e. patients that got infected somewhere else).
evidence: The claim describes established practice in the field based on common interpretation.

claim: When studying the epidemiology of antibiotic resistance, clustered strains are considered as cases of transmission of resistance, while singletons are thought to be more likely to represent instances of resistance acquisition.
source: Similarly, when studying the epidemiology of antibiotic resistance, clustered strains are considered as cases of transmission of resistance, while singletons are thought to be more likely to represent instances of resistance acquisition (Hatherell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hatherell et al., 2016.

claim: A review of more than 30 publications concluded that a threshold of six SNPs could be used to identify cases of direct transmission.
source: A review of more than 30 publications concluded that a threshold of six SNPs could be used to identify cases of direct transmission (Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019), but other studies proposed different thresholds for different settings (see Table 1 in Hatherell et al., 2016 for some examples).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019.

claim: Other studies proposed different thresholds for different settings.
source: A review of more than 30 publications concluded that a threshold of six SNPs could be used to identify cases of direct transmission (Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019), but other studies proposed different thresholds for different settings (see Table 1 in Hatherell et al., 2016 for some examples).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hatherell et al., 2016.

claim: The method proposed by Stimson et al., 2019 groups strains based on a probabilistic model that takes into account the clock rate and the time of sampling.
source: For example, the method proposed by Stimson et al., 2019 groups strains based on a probabilistic model that takes into account the clock rate and the time of sampling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stimson et al., 2019.

claim: Other studies sidestepped the choice of one specific value by performing clustering multiple times with different thresholds, and comparing the results.
source: Other studies sidestepped the choice of one specific value by performing clustering multiple times with different thresholds, and comparing the results (Holt et al., 2018; Meehan et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2018; López et al., 2020; Shuaib et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2021, Liu et al., 2021; Walter et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Many studies tested the association of clustered strains with host and bacterial sub-populations, such as different age groups, HIV-positive patients, bacterial lineages and others.
source: Many studies tested the association of clustered strains with host and bacterial sub-populations, such as different age groups, HIV-positive patients, bacterial lineages and others (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Asare et al., 2020; Sobkowiak et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2021, Gygli et al., 2021; Merker et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In these analyses, a positive association is interpreted as evidence for increased transmission of a certain sub-population.
source: In these analyses, a positive association is interpreted as evidence for increased transmission of a certain sub-population.
evidence: The claim describes the standard interpretation in the field.

claim: Holt et al., 2018 found that in Vietnam, MTB Lineage 2 (L2) had higher clustering rates compared to MTB Lineage 4 (L4) and MTB Lineage 1 (L1).
source: For example, Holt et al., 2018 found that in Vietnam, MTB Lineage 2 (L2) had higher clustering rates compared to MTB Lineage 4 (L4) and MTB Lineage 1 (L1), and interpreted these results as evidence for more frequent transmission of L2 strains, compared to L4 and L1 strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Holt et al., 2018.

claim: Holt et al., 2018 interpreted higher clustering rates of L2 as evidence for more frequent transmission of L2 strains, compared to L4 and L1 strains.
source: For example, Holt et al., 2018 found that in Vietnam, MTB Lineage 2 (L2) had higher clustering rates compared to MTB Lineage 4 (L4) and MTB Lineage 1 (L1), and interpreted these results as evidence for more frequent transmission of L2 strains, compared to L4 and L1 strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Holt et al., 2018.

claim: In recent studies the distribution of terminal branch lengths (TBL) was used as a proxy for transmissibility in different MTB lineages.
source: Finally, in recent studies the distribution of terminal branch lengths (TBL) was used as a proxy for transmissibility in different MTB lineages (Holt et al., 2018; Freschi et al., 2021; Walter et al., 2022), partially complementing classical clustering analyses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holt et al., 2018; Freschi et al., 2021; Walter et al., 2022.

claim: All approaches for clustering and TBL analyses are based on the assumption that increased transmission results in increased clustering rates and shorter terminal branches.
source: All these approaches are based on the assumption that increased transmission results in increased clustering rates and shorter terminal branches.
evidence: The claim describes the underlying assumption of the analytical approaches.

claim: It was posited that higher rates of molecular evolution and low sampling rates should lead to lower clustering rates.
source: However, it is known that other factors could influence the results of clustering, for example it was posited that higher rates of molecular evolution, and low sampling rates should lead to lower clustering rates (Stimson et al., 2019, Menardo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stimson et al., 2019, Menardo et al., 2019.

claim: Clustering results and TBL depend on many factors that have nothing to do with transmission.
source: I show that standard interpretations of this type of analyses ignore two main caveats: (1) clustering results and TBL depend on many factors that have nothing to do with transmission, (2) clustering results and TBL do not tell anything about whether the epidemic is stable, growing, or shrinking, unless all the additional parameters that influence these metrics are known, or assumed identical between sub-populations.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Clustering results and TBL do not tell anything about whether the epidemic is stable, growing, or shrinking, unless all the additional parameters that influence these metrics are known, or assumed identical between sub-populations.
source: I show that standard interpretations of this type of analyses ignore two main caveats: (1) clustering results and TBL depend on many factors that have nothing to do with transmission, (2) clustering results and TBL do not tell anything about whether the epidemic is stable, growing, or shrinking, unless all the additional parameters that influence these metrics are known, or assumed identical between sub-populations.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The optimal SNP threshold for clustering depends on the epidemiological conditions.
source: An important consequence is that the optimal SNP threshold for clustering depends on the epidemiological conditions, and that sub-populations with different epidemiological characteristics should not be analyzed with the same threshold.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results showing different optimal thresholds under different conditions.

claim: Sub-populations with different epidemiological characteristics should not be analyzed with the same threshold.
source: An important consequence is that the optimal SNP threshold for clustering depends on the epidemiological conditions, and that sub-populations with different epidemiological characteristics should not be analyzed with the same threshold.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results showing threshold dependency on epidemiological conditions.

claim: Different clustering rates and TBL distributions found consistently between different MTB lineages are probably due to intrinsic bacterial factors, and do not indicate necessarily differences in transmission or evolutionary success.
source: Finally, these results suggest that different clustering rates and TBL distributions, that are found consistently between different MTB lineages, are probably due to intrinsic bacterial factors, and do not indicate necessarily differences in transmission or evolutionary success.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results combined with observed patterns in real data.

claim: Higher clock rates led to lower clustering rates and longer TBL.
source: I found that: (1) higher clock rates led to lower clustering rates and longer TBL (Appendix 1)

claim: Lower sampling proportions resulted in lower clustering rates and longer TBL.
source: (2) lower sampling proportions resulted in lower clustering rates and longer TBL (Appendix 2)
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in Appendix 2.

claim: Shorter sampling periods resulted in lower clustering rates and longer terminal branches.
source: (3) shorter sampling periods resulted in lower clustering rates and longer terminal branches (Appendix 3).

claim: TBL and median clustering rates did not change when using a lower threshold on the minimum number of tips in the simulated tree.
source: Finally, I also tested whether different sample sizes could have an influence on the results of these analyses, and found that TBL and median clustering rates did not change when using a lower threshold on the minimum number of tips in the simulated tree (Appendix 4).
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in Appendix 4.

claim: Longer latency resulted in lower clustering rates and longer TBL.
source: I found that longer latency resulted in lower clustering rates and longer TBL (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: For long, mid, and short latency, the 95% sensitivity threshold was 10, 6, and 5 SNPs, respectively.
source: Correspondingly, the 95% sensitivity threshold was 10, 6, and 5 SNPs, and the mean of the TBL distribution was 0.87, 0.56, and 0.41, respectively for long, mid, and short latency.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in the latency analysis.

claim: For long, mid, and short latency, the mean of the TBL distribution was 0.87, 0.56, and 0.41, respectively.
source: Correspondingly, the 95% sensitivity threshold was 10, 6, and 5 SNPs, and the mean of the TBL distribution was 0.87, 0.56, and 0.41, respectively for long, mid, and short latency.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in the latency analysis.

claim: Clustering results and TBL depend on the transmission rate, with higher values leading to higher clustering rates and shorter TBL.
source: I found that clustering results and TBL depend on the transmission rate, with higher values leading to higher clustering rates and shorter TBL.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in the transmission analysis.

claim: The sampling rate had no major effect on clustering results and TBL.
source: Conversely, the sampling rate had no major effect (Appendix 5).
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in Appendix 5.

claim: R0 is the ratio between the rate at which infectious individuals are created and the rate at which infectious individuals are removed.
source: R0 is the ratio between the rate at which infectious individuals are created (numerator) and the rate at which infectious individuals are removed (denominator).
evidence: The claim is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: If the numerator is larger than the denominator the epidemic will grow (R0 >1).
source: If the numerator is larger than the denominator the epidemic will grow (R0 >1).
evidence: The claim is based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: If the denominator is larger than the numerator the epidemic will shrink (R0 <1).
source: Conversely, if the denominator is larger than the numerator the epidemic will shrink (R0 <1).
evidence: The claim is based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: With the epidemiological model used in this study, R0 = λ / (σ +ε).
source: Specifically, with the epidemiological model used in this study the numerator is the transmission rate (λ), while the denominator is determined by the sum of the sampling and death rates (σ+ε), so that R0 = λ / (σ +ε).
evidence: The claim is based on the specific epidemiological model used in the simulations.

claim: Changes in clustering rates and TBL will correlate with R0 only when the denominator (σ +ε) is fixed.
source: Because only the numerator affects the results of clustering rates and TBL, changes in these two metrics will correlate with R0 only when the denominator (σ +ε) is fixed.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results showing the effect of transmission rate.

claim: When considering scenarios with different sampling rates, and therefore infectious periods, there was no correlation between R0 and clustering rates, nor between R0 and TBL distributions.
source: When considering scenarios with different sampling rates, and therefore infectious periods, I found no correlation between R0 and clustering rates, nor between R0 and TBL distributions.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: When the duration of the infection period, and all other parameters (except the transmission rate) were fixed, larger values of R0 correlated with higher clustering rates and shorter TBL.
source: However, when the duration of the infection period, and all other parameters (except the transmission rate) were fixed, larger values of R0 correlated with higher clustering rates and shorter TBL (Table 2, Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Type 2 showed shorter terminal branches than Type 1, with mean TBL distribution of 0.4 and 0.84 SNPs respectively.
source: Type 2 showed shorter terminal branches: the mean of the TBL distribution was 0.84 and 0.4 SNPs for type 1 and type 2, respectively.

claim: Type 2 had higher clustering rates than Type 1.
source: Moreover, type 2 had higher clustering rates (Figure 4)
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The shorter TBL and larger clustering rates of type 2 are due to its shorter latency and lower clock rate, not to increased transmission.
source: However, the shorter TBL and larger clustering rates of type 2 are due to its shorter latency and lower clock rate, not to increased transmission.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results of the practical example.

claim: Type 2 has a lower transmission rate compared to type 1, and it is bound to extinction, while type 1 is growing exponentially.

claim: The length of the latent period and the clock rates used in the example are well within the range of values estimated with different data sets.

claim: The standard interpretation of clustering results and TBL distributions can potentially be misleading in some epidemiological settings.
source: Overall, these results show that the standard interpretation of clustering results and TBL distributions can potentially be misleading in some epidemiological settings.

claim: Clustering has proved to be useful to rapidly identify outbreaks and recent transmission, especially in low-incidence regions.
source: Especially in low-incidence regions, clustering has proved to be useful to rapidly identify outbreaks and recent transmission (see Walker et al., 2018 for an example).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2018.

claim: The transmission rate (per unit of time) does correlate positively with clustering rates, and negatively with TBL.
source: The results presented above demonstrate that these approaches suffer from two major limitations: (1) the transmission rate (per unit of time) does correlate positively with clustering rates, and negatively with TBL.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lengths of the latency period, the molecular clock rate, the sampling period, and the sampling proportion all influence clustering and TBL.
source: However, it is not the only factor doing so. The lengths of the latency period, the molecular clock rate, the sampling period, and the sampling proportion all influence clustering and TBL.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased clustering might be due to shorter latency, lower clock rates, longer sampling periods, or higher sampling proportion, and not to increased transmission.
source: In other words, increased clustering might be due to shorter latency, lower clock rates, longer sampling periods, or higher sampling proportion, and not to increased transmission.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results showing multiple factors affecting clustering.

claim: Whether an epidemic, or a sub-population is growing or not, depends on the ratio between the transmission rate (λ) and the rate at which infectious individuals stop being infectious (ε+σ).
source: The transmission rate expressed per unit of time does not determine the dynamic of an epidemic. Whether an epidemic, or a sub-population is growing or not, depends on the ratio between the transmission rate (λ) and the rate at which infectious individuals stop being infectious (ε+σ).
evidence: The claim is based on established epidemiological knowledge and the simulation model.

claim: Unless all other parameters are held fixed, R0 does not correlate with clustering rates or TBL.
source: Unless all other parameters are held fixed, R0 does not correlate with clustering rates or TBL.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results showing no correlation when parameters vary.

claim: TBL and clustering rates can be used to estimate whether a sub-population is stable, shrinking, or growing only by assuming that the clock rate, the latency and infectious periods, the sampling period, and the sampling proportion are identical in the two sub-populations.
source: Consequently, TBL and clustering rates can be used to estimate whether a sub-population is stable, shrinking, or growing (in relative terms compared to another sub-population), only by assuming that the clock rate, the latency and infectious periods, the sampling period, and the sampling proportion are identical in the two sub-populations.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results showing the dependency on multiple parameters.

claim: The simple comparison of clustering rates and TBL distributions without formal statistical inference disregards stochastic effects.
source: Moreover, the simple comparison of clustering rates and TBL distributions without formal statistical inference disregards stochastic effects.

claim: The same epidemiological process can generate different clustering rates and TBL.
source: The same epidemiological process can generate different clustering rates and TBL.

source: Statistical inference is necessary to test whether the observed differences are significant.

claim: The findings resonate with those of Poon, 2016, who reported that clustering methods used to study the epidemiology of HIV were biased towards detecting different sampling rates among sub-populations, and not variation in transmission rates.
source: Altogether, these results resonate with the findings of Poon, 2016, who reported that clustering methods used to study the epidemiology of HIV were biased towards detecting different sampling rates among sub-populations, and not variation in transmission rates.

claim: The change through time in the proportion of cases belonging to a certain type can be used as a proxy for the relative reproductive number.
source: For example, the change through time in the proportion of cases belonging to a certain type can be used as a proxy for the relative reproductive number (i.e. if a type is increasing in proportion within a population, it should have a larger R0 compared to other types).
evidence: The claim is based on epidemiological reasoning.

claim: If the absolute number of cases is increasing, R0 should be greater than one.
source: Similarly, if the absolute number of cases is increasing, R0 should be greater than one.
evidence: The claim is based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: The length of the infectious and latent period can be estimated (with some assumptions) from prevalence surveys and notification data.
source: Finally, the length of the infectious and latent period can be estimated (with some assumptions) from prevalence surveys and notification data (Ku et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ku et al., 2021.

claim: The 95% sensitivity SNP threshold ranged between 3 and 11 SNPs across all scenarios simulated for this study.
source: One important result is that this threshold depends strongly on the epidemiological conditions and on the sample size: across all scenarios simulated for this study the 95% sensitivity threshold ranged between 3 and 11 SNPs, and more extreme values are not impossible.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results across all scenarios.

claim: Molecular epidemiological studies should use larger thresholds for settings characterized by longer latency, lower transmission rates, shorter sampling periods, and/or lower sampling proportions.
source: Ideally, molecular epidemiological studies should use larger thresholds for settings characterized by longer latency, lower transmission rates, shorter sampling periods, and/or lower sampling proportions.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the simulation results showing threshold dependency.

claim: If a MTB population consists of sub-populations with different epidemiological characteristics, or molecular clock rates, using a single SNP threshold will lead to biased results.
source: However, if a MTB population is not uniform, but consists of sub-populations with different epidemiological characteristics, or molecular clock rates, using a single SNP threshold will lead to biased results.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results showing different optimal thresholds for different conditions.

claim: Different MTB lineages have different clustering rates and distributions of TBL, independently from the region of sampling.
source: Different MTB lineages have different clustering rates and distributions of TBL, independently from the region of sampling.
evidence: The claim is based on established patterns in the literature.

claim: Compared to other lineages, L2 was consistently found to have shorter TBL and higher clustering rates virtually everywhere, including in Vietnam, Malawi, Uzbekistan, South Africa, Georgia, Iran, as well as globally.
source: For example, compared to other lineages, L2 was consistently found to have shorter TBL and higher clustering rates virtually everywhere, including in Vietnam (Holt et al., 2018, Hang et al., 2019), Malawi (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Sobkowiak et al., 2020), Uzbekistan (Merker et al., 2018), South Africa (Cox et al., 2021), Georgia (Gygli et al., 2021), Iran (Vaziri et al., 2019), as well as globally (Freschi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies from different regions.

claim: L1 was repeatedly found to have longer terminal branches, and lower clustering rates, compared to other lineages.
source: At the opposite end of the spectrum, L1 was repeatedly found to have longer terminal branches, and lower clustering rates, compared to other lineages (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Holt et al., 2018, Hang et al., 2019, Sobkowiak et al., 2020; Freschi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The repeated pattern of different clustering and TBL between lineages is probably due to intrinsic bacterial factors, which affect clustering and TBL in all epidemiological settings.
source: This repeated pattern is probably due to intrinsic bacterial factors, which affect clustering and TBL in all epidemiological settings.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the consistent patterns observed across different regions and the simulation results.

claim: Different sampling proportions and sampling periods among lineages are unlikely to be responsible for the widespread pattern of different clustering and TBL.
source: Different sampling proportions and sampling periods among lineages are unlikely to be responsible for this widespread pattern.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the consistency of patterns across different settings.

claim: The three remaining factors that could explain the global differences between L2 and L1 are: clock rates, latency, and transmission rates per unit of time.
source: The three remaining factors that could explain the global differences between L2 and L1 are: (1) clock rates, (2) latency, and (3) transmission rates per unit of time.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results and the elimination of other factors.

claim: Different clustering results and TBL between L1 and L2 are likely caused by differences in latency and/or transmission rate per unit of time.
source: To summarize, different clustering results and TBL between L1 and L2 are likely caused by differences in latency and/or transmission rate per unit of time.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results and the analysis of lineage differences.

claim: The analysis of TBL distribution and clusters cannot tease apart differences in latency and transmission rate per unit of time.
source: However, the analysis of TBL distribution and clusters cannot tease these two factors apart.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results showing both factors have similar effects.

claim: The effects of latency, transmission, and clock rates on tree topology are additive.
source: Importantly, the effects of all these factors are additive.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: In a lineage with longer latency and lower clock rate, the longer latency would result in lower clustering rates and longer TBL, while the lower clock rate has the opposite effect.
source: For example, in a lineage with longer latency and lower clock rate, the longer latency would result in lower clustering rates and longer TBL, while the lower clock rate has the opposite effect.

claim: Clustering analyses and TBL can tell us only so much about the dynamics of MTB epidemics.
source: The take home message of this study is that clustering analyses and TBL can tell us only so much about the dynamics of MTB epidemics.

claim: Clustering will continue to be useful to detect linked strains.

source: Individuals in compartment I generate new infections adding new exposed individuals in compartment E with rate λ.

source: Exposed individuals become infectious moving from compartment E to compartment I with rate ψ.

source: Under this model the reproductive number R0 corresponds to λ/(σ+ε).
